text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Recycling has created new jobs and new raw material markets which have an annual turnover of several million crowns. The markets were set up as a three-year old law says producers, importers and retailers are responsible for taking care of their old goods.

- Swedish company Independent Media Group (IMG) -- which is active in video, music and multimedia rights -- will seek a listing on the Stockholm Stock Exchange. It needs 25 million crowns to expand on the media market in the Nordic region.

- Swedes are buying more houses and house prices keep rising. In the first half of the year, 25 percent more houses were sold than in the same period last year and house prices rose six percent. In Stockholm, house prices rose 11 percent.

- Swedish company Interaq, which builds computers out of imported hardware parts, has grown 41 percent a year since 1991. So far U.S. giants such as Compaq , IBM , Dell and AST have been market leaders in Sweden but now Swedish-built computers are taking more market share.

- It will cost Swedish banks 1.5 billion crowns to upgrade their computer systems ahead of the year 2000, a survey by the Finance Inspectorate shows. Insurers are facing similar problems while brokerages are better off.

- Companies on the innovation market almost never manage to meet their result and turnover forecasts. It is not unusual for the difference between forecasts and actual figures to be as great as 80-100 percent.
- Internet company Spray is growing very fast. "We will become one of Europe's largest Internet companies and one of the few profitable ones," its new chief executive Per Bystedt told the newspaper.

- Swedish banks and insurers are facing a hot autumn on the Stockholm Stock Exchange with merger speculation already picking up. Some of the rumours are about insurers Skandia and Trygg-Hansa and also about the bank S-E-Banken .
